title: Majestic Bishops
summary: Promote to a bishop to keep the defender moving, then use a checking move before accepting the last sacrifice.

nodes.question: Which promotion keeps Black’s win alive?
nodes.explanation: White has played Be1. A queen or rook pins that bishop and leaves the king without a legal move.

branches.title: Promote to a bishop and build the net
commentary: Black needs a promotion that preserves White’s legal moves. The pawn can become more than just a queen.
d1=B is the only winning move in this position. It avoids pinning the e1 bishop horizontally against the f1 king.
Bc3 is a legal illustrated defense. White keeps the bishop, but it cannot guard the light squares needed to stop Black’s mating net.
Bf2 restricts e1 and g1. Black’s king controls e2, f2 and g2, leaving the white king with no safe destination.
Be5 is a representative waiting move from the source idea. White’s dark-squared bishop cannot stop the light-squared net.
Be2# checks along e2-f1. Black’s king and other bishop cover every escape, and the white bishop cannot capture the checker.
branches.classification: independent alternative illustrating a source idea with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Be2# checks along e2-f1. Black’s king and other bishop cover every escape, and the white bishop cannot capture the checker.

branches.title: Try the usual queen promotion
commentary: Before choosing the strongest piece, count the defender’s legal moves after promotion.
d1=Q is immediate stalemate: Be1 is pinned to Kf1, while Black’s king and bishop take away all king moves. White is not in check, so the game is drawn.
branches.explanation: d1=Q is immediate stalemate: Be1 is pinned to Kf1, while Black’s king and bishop take away all king moves. White is not in check, so the game is drawn.

branches.title: Does a rook avoid stalemate?
commentary: A rook has fewer moves than a queen, but here it creates the same horizontal pin.
d1=R still pins Be1 against Kf1. White has no legal king or bishop move and is not checked: stalemate again.
branches.explanation: d1=R still pins Be1 against Kf1. White has no legal king or bishop move and is not checked: stalemate again.

branches.title: Try a knight and White’s distant defense
commentary: A knight avoids the pin, but avoiding stalemate is only the first condition for a winning promotion.
d1=N gives up the forced win. The new knight cannot force the opposing bishop into capture against best defense.
Ba5 keeps White’s bishop away from the knight’s immediate reach. The exact tablebase result is a draw.
branches.explanation: Ba5 keeps White’s bishop away from the knight’s immediate reach. The exact tablebase result is a draw.

branches.title: Accept the bishop sacrifice immediately
commentary: White can try another sacrifice after the bishop promotion. Ask what taking it does to the last king moves.
d1=B keeps Black’s winning position.
Bf2 offers White’s bishop. Capturing with the c5 bishop would remove White’s only movable piece.
Bxf2 is stalemate. The new bishop on d1 does not check Kf1, and Black’s king and f2 bishop deny every escape.
branches.explanation: Bxf2 is stalemate. The new bishop on d1 does not check Kf1, and Black’s king and f2 bishop deny every escape.

branches.title: Check before accepting the sacrifice
commentary: Compare accepting Bf2 immediately with changing the king’s square first.
d1=B chooses the winning promotion.
Bf2 is the defender’s stalemate attempt.
Be2+ forces the king to move before Black captures the bishop. This changes the geometry of the stalemate trap.
Ke1 is one legal representative response; it is not claimed to be the only move.
Bxf2+ captures with check after the king has moved. Black retains two bishops of opposite colors against a bare king, a verified win.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Bxf2+ captures with check after the king has moved. Black retains two bishops of opposite colors against a bare king, a verified win.

exercises.prompt: Why do queen and rook promotion both draw?
exercises.answer: They pin Be1 horizontally against Kf1. The bishop cannot move legally, and Black’s king and c5 bishop already control every king escape.
Moving White’s king prevents the immediate-capture stalemate. After the king moves, Black can take the bishop and keep a winning two-bishop ending.

startContext: Play Black from the position after ...d2 and Be1. The initial pawn push is source context; the promotion choice and selected replies are checked here.
verification_scope: The playable starting position and every intermediate position in the selected variations are tablebase-checked. These variations illustrate the key ideas; they do not enumerate all legal defenses.
